turns.content: hey man... can i ask you something kinda random? i had dinner last night with my friend tariq, weve been close since college. he just got a great job after months of unemployment. i was happy for him, really. but when i tried to tell him my dad needs triple bypass surgery next week, he literally pulled out his phone mid-sentence to check fantasy football and changed the subject. never came back to it. am i crazy for feeling insulted?

No, man—you’re not crazy for feeling insulted. You were trying to tell a close friend something scary about your dad, and he checked fantasy football and changed the subject. That would hurt, especially from someone you’ve been close to since college.

You can be genuinely happy about his new job **and** need him to show up for you. Those aren’t competing things.

This one moment doesn’t tell you everything about Tariq or your friendship—he might’ve been distracted or not known how to respond—but you don’t have to explain away the impact. If you want to bring it up, you could say:

“Hey, when I mentioned my dad’s surgery last night and you checked your phone and changed the subject, I felt brushed off. I’m worried about him, and I needed you to listen.”

How he responds will tell you more than guessing at why he did it.

How are you holding up with your dad’s surgery coming up?

yeah... i hear you. i know you're saying talk to him about it. but the thing is, i spent four months being this ultra-attentive listener for him. i even read that article about how to be a good listener - you know, remember names, don't interrupt, don't make it about yourself. i did all of it. and he couldn't give me two minutes.

Yeah—that’s what makes it sting. You spent four months making room for what he was going through, and when you needed two minutes for something frightening, he didn’t give you that attention.

You weren’t listening to him to earn a favor later. But **expecting some mutual care in a close friendship isn’t keeping score.** You shouldn’t have to be a perfect listener—or follow an article’s checklist—to deserve being heard about your dad’s surgery.

And I moved a little quickly to “talk to him.” You don’t have to turn being hurt into another assignment where you carefully manage the conversation. It’s okay to feel let down and not decide what to do about Tariq right now.

Is there someone else you can lean on this week—someone you don’t have to work so hard to be heard by?

thanks man. i appreciate you saying i dont have to decide right now. i keep replaying the fantasy football thing in my head... like i was mid-sentence about my dad's heart and he laughed at a trade notification. that image is stuck.

Yeah, man. You were mid-sentence about your dad’s heart, and he was laughing at something on his phone. That’s a painful contrast—no wonder that particular moment keeps coming back.

Even if his laughter was about the trade, not your dad, it still left you alone with something scary right when you were reaching out. You don’t have to prove he meant to hurt you for it to hurt.

When the image comes up, you might gently name what’s underneath it: **“I’m scared about Dad, and I needed my friend to be there.”** Not to make the feeling disappear—just to give yourself somewhere to land besides replaying what he did.

Do you want to tell me about your dad—what’s worrying you most about next week?

yeah... the fantasy football thing is like burned into my brain now. i keep thinking i should just send him a text calling him out. something like "hey remember when you pulled out your phone while i was telling you about my dad's surgery?" but part of me thinks i'm making it too big in my head.

You’re not making it too big by wanting to address it. Your dad’s surgery is a big deal, and being brushed off by a close friend hurt. The replay may be making that hurt feel fresh, but it isn’t inventing it.

Your draft is understandable. If you want to make the point clear without opening with a sarcastic question, you could say:

> “Hey, something from dinner has been bothering me. When I was telling you about my dad’s surgery, you checked fantasy football and changed the subject. I felt really brushed off. I’m scared about next week, and I needed you to listen.”

That names what happened without deciding what his intentions were. You don’t need to lay out all four months of support for this request to be reasonable.

**You can write it now and decide later whether to send it.** There’s no deadline, and you don’t have to be completely over the hurt before you bring it up.
yeah... i just don't know if i have the energy to send that and then wait for his reply. or if i even want to hear whatever excuse he comes up with. maybe i just let the friendship fade out quietly.

Yeah—the text isn’t just a text. It’s waiting for the reply, wondering whether he gets it, and possibly having another exhausting conversation while you’re already worried about your dad. It makes sense that you don’t have room for that.

**You can take space without deciding the friendship is over.** For now, that might mean not initiating contact and putting your energy toward your dad and people who can support you. That’s a pause, not a punishment.

Letting the friendship fade is an option, too. But you don’t have to choose between confronting him today and quietly ending things forever. After the surgery, you might want to hear him out—or you might still want distance. Either way, you’re allowed to leave this unresolved while you get through next week.
